displayQuote: In war there is no substitute for victory

meta.title: Who really said "In war there is no substitute for victory"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, MacArthur said it to Congress on April 19, 1951, though the printed Congressional Record reads “there can be no substitute for victory.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In war there is no substitute for victory'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, MacArthur said it to Congress on April 19, 1951, though the printed Congressional Record reads “there can be no substitute for victory.”

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Said in his address to a joint session of Congress on April 19, 1951. The popular wording matches a transcription of the speech audio, and the official Congressional Record prints it as “In war, indeed, there can be no substitute for victory.” He had already written the shorter “There is no substitute for victory” in a letter of March 20, 1951.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Address to a joint session of Congress (the “Farewell Address”)
Congressional Record, vol. 97, pt. 3, p. 4125 (the address begins on p. 4123)
Letter to Rep. Joseph W. Martin Jr., Tokyo, March 20, 1951

source.excerpt: But once war is forced upon us, there is no other alternative than to apply every available means to bring it to a swift end. War’s very object is victory, not prolonged indecision. In war there is no substitute for victory.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced material on MacArthur, under “Farewell address to Congress (1951)”, and gives the shorter form from his letter to Joseph Martin: Wikiquote: Douglas MacArthur ↗.

The letter, dated Tokyo, March 20, 1951 and read in the House on April 5, ends: “As you pointed out, we must win. There is no substitute for victory.” Foreign Relations of the United States, 1951, vol. VII, pt. 1, doc. 206 ↗.
The official text of the April 19 address prints the sentence on p. 4125 as “In war, indeed, there can be no substitute for victory.” Congressional Record scan, congress.gov ↗.
A transcription made from the speech audio gives the popular wording, “In war there is no substitute for victory.” American Rhetoric ↗.
source.excerptNote: Spoken text as transcribed from the audio by American Rhetoric ↗. The official Congressional Record ↗ prints the sentence as “In war, indeed, there can be no substitute for victory.”
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Douglas MacArthur (status unresolved; see note)
source.rightsNote: The address was delivered and printed in 1951, so under our conservative rule we treat it as in copyright and do not claim public domain. Its Congressional Record printing is a U.S. government publication, and we have not determined whether the speech itself counts as a government work. Quoting one sentence for commentary is a short excerpt.

author.name: Douglas MacArthur
author.heading: About Douglas MacArthur
author.bio: Douglas MacArthur was an American general. He led Allied forces in the Southwest Pacific in the Second World War and later commanded United Nations forces in Korea. President Truman relieved him of his commands on April 11, 1951 ↗. On April 19 he made his case before Congress in the speech that contains this line.

misattribution.heading: Three wordings, one speaker
misattribution.intro: The attribution is genuine. What varies is the wording: MacArthur used the idea at least twice in 1951, and the printed record of his speech does not match what he said aloud word for word.

items.who: “In war there is no substitute for victory”
items.why: This is what he said aloud to Congress, according to a transcription made from the audio ↗.

items.who: “In war, indeed, there can be no substitute for victory”
items.why: This is how the Congressional Record ↗ (vol. 97, pt. 3, p. 4125) prints it. So “can be” versions in print are not wrong. They follow the official text.
This comes from his letter to Rep. Joseph W. Martin Jr., which Martin read in the House on April 5, 1951 (FRUS 1951, vol. VII, pt. 1, doc. 206 ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: All three wordings are MacArthur’s own, from 1951. The popular “In war there is no substitute for victory” matches his spoken address to Congress on April 19, 1951. The printed Congressional Record ↗ adds “indeed” and “can be.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: MacArthur’s letter to Rep. Joseph Martin, with its “There is no substitute for victory,” was read on the House floor on April 5, 1951 ↗. On April 11 President Truman relieved him of his commands ↗, saying MacArthur could not give his “wholehearted support” to U.S. and U.N. policy.

On April 19 MacArthur addressed Congress and repeated the idea as part of his case against a limited war in Korea. That speech also ended with “old soldiers never die; they just fade away,” and the line became one of the best-known slogans of the Truman–MacArthur dispute.
context.detailsSummary: What this page does not claim
detailsBody: This page documents MacArthur’s own 1951 uses of the phrase. We have not traced whether anyone used “no substitute for victory” before him, so we do not say he coined it.
Quote Investigator has not published an article on this line. Our anchor is Wikiquote’s sourced entries, checked against the Congressional Record and the State Department’s Foreign Relations series.
